items.bron: Fiveable, 'Frame structure' (Intro to Civil Engineering): a framework of connected parts that carries loads; DBE 2026 ATP NST Gr 4, 'Struts and frame structures'.

items.bewering: In Kwartaal 1 het jy gesien 'n raamstruktuur is los dele wat aanmekaar sit met oop plekke tussen hulle.
items.bron: The reference to Term 1 holds: DBE 2026 ATP NST Gr 4, Term 1 'Structures for animal shelters' says 'animal shelters can be shell or frame structures'. The description does not hold as a definition. Fiveable 'Frame structure' describes connected parts that carry loads and keep the shape. 'Los dele wat aanmekaar sit met oop plekke tussen hulle' also fits a chain, a string of beads or a bead curtain, none of which is a frame structure. It says nothing about the parts being stiff or about the frame keeping a shape or carrying weight.
items.regstelling: Keep the reference to Term 1, but make the description say what makes a frame a frame. For example: a frame structure is stiff parts (struts) joined together so that together they keep a shape or carry weight, with open spaces between them. The same fix applies to the glossary entry 'raamstruktuur'. If this wording is shared with other lessons, it has to change everywhere at once.

items.bewering: 'n Raam gee die maklikste in op die plek waar twee stutte aanmekaar sit.
items.bron: TeachEngineering, 'Triangles & Trusses': a square changes shape because the angle at the joints changes while the parts stay the same length. That supports the claim for frames whose joints can turn, such as the paper tubes and tape in CAPS. But Wikipedia 'Moment-resisting frame' and 'Rigid frame' show that many real building frames have stiff joints made specifically so they do not turn. There the joint is not necessarily where the frame gives way first. As a statement about every frame, the superlative does not hold.
items.regstelling: Narrow the quantifier. For example: 'n Raam gee dikwels die maklikste in op die plek waar twee stutte aanmekaar sit (or: 'n Raam waarvan die stutte by die verbindings kan draai, gee die maklikste daar in).

items.bewering: Die twee stutte kan by daardie plek teen mekaar draai.
items.bron: TeachEngineering, 'Triangles & Trusses' ('racking': the angle between parts changes at the joint).

items.bewering: Sit vier stutte in 'n vierkant aanmekaar. Hou die onderste stut stil en druk teen die boonste hoek. Die vierkant staan skeef en lê nou soos 'n leunende ruit. Nie een van die vier stutte het langer of korter geword nie. Die stutte het net by hul verbindings gedraai en die vorm het verander.
items.bron: TeachEngineering, 'Triangles & Trusses': push against a square and it becomes a rhombus, because the angle between the parts can change without the parts getting longer, shorter or bending. ASCE-ville, 'Why is the triangle the strongest shape' says the same. This holds for joints that can turn, which the previous block has already set up.

items.bewering: Sit nou drie stutte in 'n driehoek aanmekaar. Hou weer die onderste stut stil en druk net so hard teen die boonste hoek. Niks aan die driehoek se vorm verander nie.
items.bron: ASCE-ville, 'Why is the triangle the strongest shape'; TeachEngineering, 'Triangles & Trusses': once its side lengths are fixed, a triangle is rigid. 'Net so hard' keeps the comparison fair and does not claim the triangle can never fail.

items.bewering: 'n Driehoek kan net van vorm verander as een van sy stutte langer of korter word. Elke stut is styf en bly net so lank as wat hy was.
items.bron: TeachEngineering, 'Triangles & Trusses': 'The angle between two sides of the triangle is based on the length of the opposite side'. The side lengths fix the angles, so the shape can change only if a side changes length (or a part bends). The mechanism is right, and it covers both longer and shorter, which matters because in a triangle that is being pushed some parts are pulled.

items.bewering: Bouers sit daarom driehoeke in 'n raam om hom sterk en stabiel te hou.
items.bron: Wikipedia 'Truss'; TeachEngineering, 'Triangles & Trusses' (triangles as bracing in frames).

items.bron: Wikipedia 'Timber roof truss'; Build-Construct, 'Roof truss anatomy'. One note, not an error: in engineering, the bottom beam of a roof truss (the tie beam or ceiling joist) is pulled, not pushed, so strictly it is not a 'strut' as this lesson defines one. CAPS itself calls all the parts struts, so this is a curriculum convention and I have not flagged it.

items.bewering: Die teëls of die plate lê bo-op hom en jy sien hom gewoonlik nie.
items.bron: Naicker et al. 2017, 'Indoor temperatures in low cost housing in Johannesburg' (PMC5708049): 93% of the RDP houses in Braamfischerville and 75% of the informal homes at Hospital Hill had no ceiling, and ceilings were 'lacking in low cost dwellings built prior to 2015'. EBRD Green Cities, Cape Town ceiling retrofitting programme: thousands of RDP houses were built without ceilings. In a house with no ceiling you can see the roof frame, so for a large group of South African learners 'you usually don't see it' is not true. The first half (tiles or sheets lie on the roof frame) holds (Wikipedia 'Timber roof truss').
items.regstelling: Tie 'you don't see it' to a ceiling rather than to 'usually'. For example: Die teëls of die plate lê bo-op hom. In 'n huis met 'n plafon sit hy bo die plafon en sien jy hom nie. Or cut the clause.

items.bron: Cambridge Dictionary, 'crane': 'a big machine with a long arm that is used ... for lifting and moving heavy things'; Wikipedia 'Crane (machine)'. It leaves out that a crane also moves loads sideways, but it is not false.

items.bron: SANY Global, 'Which two cranes typically use a lattice boom'; FridayParts, same topic: a lattice boom is a frame of steel tubes built on triangles, and it weighs much less than a solid boom of the same length.

items.bron: SANY Global and Almarwan, 'Lattice boom vs telescopic boom': a telescopic boom is made of solid steel box sections that slide inside one another.

items.bewering: 'n Kragmas is die hoë staalraam wat die kragdrade oor die land dra. Sy dun stutte staan in driehoeke van die grond tot heel bo.
items.bron: Eskom, Final Basic Assessment Report, Olien-Karats 132kV powerline (eskom.co.za, 2025): the pylon proposed is 'a single circuit steel mono-pole structure'. Eskom, Oasis-Taaipit 132kV FBAR: wooden pole structures replaced with steel monopoles. Eskom EIA documents also talk about 'monopole pylons'. Many pylons in South Africa are therefore a single thick steel pole with no triangles (and some lines still run on wooden poles). The lattice frame in triangles is true of many pylons (Eskom 400kV tower specifications, self-supporting lattice towers), but not of all. In contrast, the block handles cranes correctly with 'party' and 'ander'.
items.regstelling: Narrow the quantifier, as the crane sentences already do. For example: Baie kragmaste is hoë staalrame wat die kragdrade oor die land dra. Hulle dun stutte staan in driehoeke van die grond tot heel bo. Ander kragmaste is net een dik staalpaal.

items.bewering: 'n Geraamte is die raam binne-in die lyf van 'n dier met 'n ruggraat.
items.bron: Wikipedia 'Skeleton': 'A skeleton is the structural frame that supports the body of most animals'. Its types include the exoskeleton (a stiff outer shell) and the endoskeleton. Britannica Kids, 'exoskeleton': 'The word exoskeleton means outside skeleton'. UCMP Berkeley, 'Morphology of Echinodermata': starfish and sea urchins have an internal skeleton and no backbone. The sentence is true of vertebrates, but as a definition it claims that only a frame inside a backbone animal counts as a skeleton, so an insect or crab has no skeleton. Biology says they do.
items.regstelling: Do not make 'with a backbone' part of the definition. For example: 'n Geraamte is die harde raam wat 'n dier se lyf ophou. By 'n dier met 'n ruggraat sit die geraamte binne-in die lyf. The last sentence of the block ('Party diere ... dra 'n harde dop buite') can then stay, or say that their skeleton is on the outside.

items.bewering: Die lang harde dele binne 'n dier se pote werk soos stutte. Hulle dra die dier se gewig en hou hom op sy pote.
items.bron: DBE 2026 ATP NST Gr 4 ('limb bones are struts'); TRU Human Anatomy & Physiology I, 'Biomechanics', and PMC5601257, 'Mechanical basis of bone strength': bones carry compression and muscles supply the pull. The mapping holds: bone is to animal what strut is to frame, and the lesson itself says straight away where the comparison ends (joints that turn, bands and muscles). Limb bones are also bent, not only pushed, but that does not make the comparison mislead at this level.

items.bewering: Die stutte van 'n geraamte staan nie in driehoeke nie.
items.bron: I could not settle it either way. For: limb bones meet at movable joints and are held by ligaments and muscles, not by fixed triangles (NCBI InformedHealth, 'How does the knee work?'; Merck Manual, 'Ligaments'). Against the absolute 'nie': a bird's coracoid braces the shoulder against the breastbone like a strut, and the scapula, coracoid and furcula are tightly bound together (PMC9023055, eLife 76086). D'Arcy Thompson and UCSD (Meyers group, 'Reinforcing structures in avian wing bones') describe struts in triangles like a Warren truss inside vulture wing bones. Several biomechanics texts treat bones as parts under compression and muscles as parts under tension working together. I also point out, without judging the lesson against it, that the curriculum text (DBE 2026 ATP) lists skeletons among the examples where 'struts are joined into triangular shapes'. The lesson says the opposite outright. I found no reference source that states either version for the skeleton as a whole. A person needs to decide whether the claim is narrowed (for example to the bones in the legs, which turn at joints instead of standing in triangles), softened, or cut.

items.bewering: Hulle kom by gewrigte bymekaar en kan by daardie plekke draai.
items.bron: StatPearls, 'Anatomy, Joints' (NCBI NBK507893); TeachMeAnatomy, 'Classification of joints': limb bones meet at synovial joints, which move freely.

items.bewering: Sterk bande hou die stutte by die gewrigte saam en spiere keer dat 'n gewrig vou.
items.bron: Merck Manual, 'Ligaments' (ligaments bind bones together at joints and make them stable); Arthritis Foundation, 'Anatomy of the knee' and InformedHealth (NCBI): muscles support the knee and stop it buckling.

items.bron: Britannica Kids, 'exoskeleton'; Britannica, 'Arthropod: form and function' (insects, crabs and spiders have a hard outer covering).

items.bron: Designing Buildings Wiki, 'Strut'; Wikipedia 'Compression member'. True on its own. (See the note on roof trusses: engineering calls a part that is pulled a tie, not a strut. CAPS's convention is broader.)

items.bewering: raamstruktuur: Los dele wat aanmekaar sit met oop plekke tussen hulle.
items.bron: Fiveable, 'Frame structure': connected parts that carry loads and keep the shape. On its own, this entry fits things that are not frame structures, such as a chain, a string of beads or a bead curtain. It leaves out that the parts are stiff and that together they keep a shape or carry weight. 'Los dele' can also be read as 'loose parts', which is exactly what a frame's parts are not.
items.regstelling: For example: Stywe dele (stutte) wat aanmekaar sit en saam 'n vorm hou of 'n gewig dra, met oop plekke tussen hulle. Change it in the study text in 'Stutte word aanmekaar gesit' too, and in every other lesson if the wording is shared.

items.bron: Wikipedia 'Timber roof truss'; Build-Construct, 'Roof truss anatomy'. True on its own.

items.bron: Cambridge Dictionary, 'crane' ('a big machine with a long arm ... for lifting and moving heavy things'); Wikipedia 'Crane (machine)'. True on its own.

items.bewering: kragmas: 'n Hoë staalraam wat kragdrade bo die grond dra.
items.bron: Eskom FBAR Olien-Karats 132kV and Oasis-Taaipit 132kV (eskom.co.za): steel monopole pylons, which are one pole, not a frame. Wooden poles are also used. On its own, this entry excludes every pylon that is not a lattice frame.
items.regstelling: For example: 'n Hoë mas wat kragdrade bo die grond dra. Baie kragmaste is staalrame. (Narrow the quantifier on 'staalraam'; do not drop the subject.)

items.bewering: geraamte: Die raam binne-in die lyf van 'n dier met 'n ruggraat, wat hom ophou.
items.bron: Wikipedia 'Skeleton' (exoskeletons and endoskeletons are both skeletons; a skeleton supports the body of most animals); Britannica Kids, 'exoskeleton' ('outside skeleton'); UCMP Berkeley, echinoderms (internal skeleton, no backbone). On its own, the entry says an insect, crab or starfish has no skeleton.
items.regstelling: For example: Die harde raam wat 'n dier se lyf ophou. By 'n dier met 'n ruggraat is dit binne-in die lyf.

items.bewering: stabiel: Iets is stabiel as dit sy vorm hou wanneer jy teen dit druk.
items.bron: Galileo Educational Network, 'Structures: Stability': 'A structure that will not topple over easily when acted upon by a force is called a stable structure'. AboutCivil, 'Structural stability': stability is resistance to sliding, collapsing and overturning. On its own, the entry calls a tall, stiff box that keeps its shape but falls over when pushed 'stable'. It covers only half of what the word means.
items.regstelling: For example: Iets is stabiel as dit nie omval nie en sy vorm hou wanneer jy teen dit druk.

items.bewering: gewrig: Die plek waar twee harde dele in 'n lyf kan draai.
items.bron: StatPearls, 'Anatomy, Joints' (NCBI NBK507893): 'A joint is a region where 2 bones make contact', and joints may be immovable, slightly movable or freely movable. Biology Online and TeachMeAnatomy: skull sutures are joints that do not move. On its own, the entry makes turning part of what a joint is, so a joint that does not move would not count.
items.regstelling: For example: Die plek waar twee harde dele in 'n lyf bymekaarkom. By baie gewrigte kan hulle draai. (Narrow the quantifier on 'draai'; do not drop the subject.)

opsomming: The triangle-versus-square mechanism is right, but a person has to decide on the absolute claim that a skeleton's struts do not stand in triangles, which I could not settle and which the curriculum text itself contradicts; ten other claims across six topics need a fix: a pylon is not always a frame of triangles (Eskom uses steel monopoles), many South African homes have no ceiling so the roof frame is visible, 'the easiest' place a frame gives way is too absolute, and the descriptions of frame structure, skeleton, stable and joint are too narrow or too broad when read alone (frame structure, skeleton and pylon are each wrong in both the study text and the glossary).
